extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy (Aristotle / Nicomachean Ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and distinguishing Aristotelian moral categories (self-control, vice, pleasure, friendship) and the criteria by which characters/states are judged good or bad. Emphasises how desires, reason, pleasure, and social goods determine moral evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-Control (enkrateia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The state in which a person "abides by [his] conclusions and moral choice" and does not change them under the sway of passion; actual mastery rather than merely continued resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-Control is more choice-worthy than Endurance; it consists in actual mastery (not merely not being conquered). The self-controlled person may feel bad desires but does not yield to them; he is the mean between the man who takes too little pleasure and the man who takes too much. He is entitled to the designation 'self-controlled' per se only when he abides by true opinion (right moral choice), not merely by any opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect Self-Control (akrasia, weak self-control)
rubrics_metrics.description: A character who follows bodily pleasures in excess and in defiance of Right Reason, 'without acting on any deliberate conviction'; yields to passion though not convinced that excess is proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imperfect Self-Control is distinguished from utter lack of self-control by the presence of remorse and the preservation of the highest principle (reason). Two forms: Precipitancy (no resolutions formed) and Weakness (resolutions formed but broken by passion). It is often curable (like an acute disorder) and more forgivable when arising from sudden temptation than from settled irresolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utter Absence of Self-Control (prospathia to self-mastery absent / continence absent)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who acts upon a conviction that following bodily pleasures without limit is proper; he 'acts upon a conviction which rests on his natural inclination' and thus lacks remorse and is incurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This state differs in kind from Imperfect Self-Control: the utterly self-indulgent person is a confirmed vice who preserves corrupt moral principle and therefore is far more harmful; unlike the imperfectly self-controlled, he acts from conviction rather than being overcome against his better judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precipitancy vs Weakness (forms of imperfect self-control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Precipitancy: led by passion because no resolutions were formed; Weakness: resolutions are formed but not kept because of passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precipitancy is common in those of sharp or melancholic temperament (swift or violent passions). Those who form resolutions and break them (weakness) are often more difficult to cure by habit; the precipitate may be less blameworthy in certain respects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remorse as moral indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of remorse indicates Imperfect Self-Control and the possibility of cure; absence of remorse indicates utter depravity/incurability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'man utterly destitute of Self-Control is not given to remorse' and is therefore incurable; the imperfectly self-controlled is 'almost made up of remorse,' making reform possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anger vs Lust (comparative disgrace)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anger follows Reason in a manner and is relatively open; Lust does not follow Reason and is insidious and more disgraceful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because anger often emerges as a response to perceived insolence and involves pain when acting, it is less disgraceful than lust-driven vice, which is pleasurable and insidious. Thus Imperfect Self-Control arising from Lust is judged worse than that arising from Anger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Softness vs Endurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Softness: the character who yields to pleasures/pains which common people would resist (including being 'slave to amusement'); Endurance: continued resistance to pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endurance is resistance over time; Self-Control is active mastery — they are distinct virtues. Softness is often due to seeking relaxation or avoiding trouble and is culpable when it leads to excess (Luxury is a kind of Softness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Excusability: natural/common desires and degree
rubrics_metrics.description: Following desires that are natural, common to the species, or within commonly shared degree is more excusable than following brutish or pathological desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some desires are proper to human nature (and may be objects of Perfected Self-Mastery), others are brutish or disease-caused. Excess of natural desires is still blameworthy, but conformity to species-typical desires in normal degree mitigates blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntariness, deliberation, and moral responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes actions done from impulse, from slight impulse, or from deliberate conviction; voluntary action and deliberation affect moral judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doing something 'without any impulse of desire' (or with very slight one) is worse than doing the same from a strong impulse, since the former implies baseness in moral choice. The nature of the motive (noble vs base pleasure) alters moral assessment (e.g., Neoptolemus' action motivated by a noble pleasure is not simply akratic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Wisdom (phronesis) vs Cleverness
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical Wisdom entails goodness of moral character and aptitude for action (right moral choice); Cleverness is intellectual skill but may coexist with Imperfect Self-Control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One cannot be both a man of Practical Wisdom and of Imperfect Self-Control, since Practical Wisdom presupposes moral excellence; cleverness might be present without the moral aptitude for right action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per se (simply) vs incidentally abiding by conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: A person is 'self-controlled per se' only if he abides by true conclusions and right moral choice; incidentally means abiding by conclusions of any kind (even false) because they lead to some other end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The correct attribution of 'self-controlled' or 'imperfect' should be made with respect to whether the person adheres to true opinion/right moral choice, not merely any settled opinion or resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Pleasures (bodily vs intellectual/active)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures are of different kinds: bodily pleasures (often accompanied by desire and pain, liable to excess) vs pleasures that are 'active workings' of the intellect or the natural state (which need not be processes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all pleasures are bad or mere processes; some pleasures (e.g., of contemplative intellect) are active workings and choice-worthy. Bodily pleasures are common to brutes and children and more liable to be low or excessive. Distinguish pleasures that cure a deficiency (remedial) from those that are naturally pleasant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for a Pleasure being good
rubrics_metrics.description: A pleasure is good per se if it is an unimpeded active working of a natural state, not merely a process toward an end or a remedial cure; some pleasures are choice-worthy, others low or harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure that accompanies the full exercise of a human power (e.g., contemplative activity) is genuinely good. Pleasures that are violent, remedial, or merely bodily may be bad in excess but not necessarily bad simpliciter. The happy life’s active workings are pleasurable, so certain pleasures are integral to Happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure's relation to Happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure accompanies the active working of a nature; since Happiness is perfect active working, pleasure is naturally interwoven with the happy life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though some argue Pleasure is not the Chief Good, Aristotle holds that pleasure (of the right kind) may be part of the Chief Good because it indicates unimpeded activity; external goods are nonetheless necessary additions so activity is not fettered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why bodily pleasures seem most choice-worthy (explanatory criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodily pleasures appear superior because they drive out pain, often act as violent remedies, and are most frequently experienced (esp. in youth or certain temperaments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explanatory account of error — it is not a normative endorsement. Recognize predispositions (youth, melancholic temperament, habituation) that make bodily pleasures seem attractive, which helps diagnose akratic behavior and moral weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of Friendship (good, pleasurable, useful)
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship has as its object what is good, or pleasurable, or useful; people feel friendship toward what appears good to them (good to the individual) as well as toward the abstract good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish whether friendship is oriented to absolute good or to what is good for the individual; typically each individual loves what appears good to him. Friendship is necessary, honourable, and a bond of communities; legislators prize it even over Justice for social cohesion.
